Everything is Just MatMul: Mastering Cache Locality Before You Write CUDA

Pre-Requisites : Basic C++ (loops, pointers.I'm learning too, lol), familiarity with PyTorch Tensors. Maybe read the first 20 odd pages of Ulrich Drepper's paper, "What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory." That’s about it
It all starts with why matrix multiplication is such a big deal I mean, it’s just matrix multiplication. It was my favorite thing to do in 10th grade and the only thing that i was good at, but little did I know back in 2021 that I’d soon witness November 30th, 2022 the day ChatGPT dropped and changed the world as I knew it. And under the hood? It’s all driven by matrix multiplication. Matmul is the single most important operation in all of deep learning. Every linear layer, every attention score, every MLP projection they all reduce to it. When engineers say "make inference faster," what they almost always mean is "make matmul faster." Optimizing this one operation means optimizing the core of AI itself. So, I decided to build it from scratch. I wrote three different versions, benchmarked them on my M3 Mac, and here is exactly what I learned.
When we first learn about matrices, we picture them as a 2D grid of rows and columns. That’s how we visualize it, but a computer sees it completely differently. Your computer's memory isn't a grid it's just one incredibly long, flat line of bytes. So, when we store a 2D matrix, we have to flatten it out using what we call row major layout. This basically means we lay out Row 0 completely in memory, followed immediately by Row 1, then Row 2, and so on. Because we are forcing a 2D grid into a 1D line, accessing an element requires us to calculate its exact flat position using a simple formula
Index = (row * number_of_columns) + column
So we have three different approaches to implement this formula All three compute the same thing: C[i][j] = sum of A[i][k] * B[k][j] for all k. Same O(n³) complexity. But the memory access patterns are completely different. Lets start with the naive approach

The Naive Approach

Alright, here's the most straightforward way to multiply two matrices. No tricks, no optimization  just three nested loops doing exactly what the math textbook says
cpp
Matrix naive_matmul(const Matrix& A, const Matrix& B){
    if(A.columns != B.rows){
        std :: cout << "The matrix multiplication is not possible due to dimensional mismatch";
        return Matrix();
    }

    int A_r = A.rows;
    int A_c = A.columns;
    int B_c = B.columns;

    Matrix result(A_r,B_c);
    result.zeros();

    for(int i =0; i < A_r; i++){
        for(int j = 0; j<B_c; j++){
            for(int k = 0; k < A_c ; k++){
                result.at(i,j) += A.at(i,k) * B.at(k,j);
            }
        }
    }
    return result;
}
i and j are our destination coordinates they lock in the exact cell we are trying to calculate in our final result matrix. The outer loop i picks the row and the middle loop j picks the column k is the slider the innermost loop k is the absolute workhorse of this operation.
So when we are computing c[0][0]  we need Row 0 of A : [1,2,3] and Column 0 of B [2,3,1] reading down The k loop goes: k=0, k=1, k=2:
  • k=0: C[0][0] += A[0][0] * B[0][0] → C[0][0] += 1 * 2 = 2
  • k=1: C[0][0] += A[0][1] * B[1][0] → C[0][0] += 2 * 3 = 6 (this is the iteration shown in the diagram above)
  • k=2: C[0][0] += A[0][2] * B[2][0] → C[0][0] += 3 * 1 = 3
Final result - C[0][0] = 2 + 6 + 3 = 11 remember from earlier matrices are stored flat in row-major order. The formula is index = row * num_cols + col
A[i][k] - As k increments (0 -> 1 -> 2), we're moving right across the row. The flat index goes i*N + 0, i*N + 1, i*N + 2 consecutive memory positions. This is sequential access. One cache line (64 bytes = 16 floats) covers multiple accesses.
For B[k][j] - As k increments (0 -> 1 -> 2), we're moving down the column. The flat index goes 0*N + j, 1*N + j, 2*N + j jumping by N positions each time. For N=1024, that's jumping 1024 floats = 4096 bytes = 64 cache lines away. This is strided access.
The problem: Every time we access B[k][j] with a new k, we're loading a completely new cache line from memory. The CPU loads 16 floats into cache, we use one, then immediately jump 1024 positions away and load another cache line. We are wasting 15 out of every 16 floats we load. This is why the naive version is slow. Not because the math is wrong the math is perfect but because the memory access pattern is fighting against how the CPU cache works.

The Cache Optimised Version (I-k-j)

cpp
Matrix cache_optimised(const Matrix& A, const Matrix& B){
    if(A.columns != B.rows){
        std :: cout << "The matrix multiplication is not possible due to dimensional mismatch";
        return Matrix();
    }

    int A_r = A.rows;
    int A_c = A.columns;
    int B_c = B.columns;

    Matrix result(A_r, B_c);
    result.zeros();
    for(int i = 0; i < A_r; i++){
        for(int k = 0; k < A_c; k++){
            float A_val = A.at(i,k); // load once and reuse n times
            for(int j = 0; j<B_c; j++){
                result.at(i,j) += A_val * B.at(k,j);
            }
        }
    }
    return result;

}
Instead of i-j-k, it's now i-k-j. That's it. Same math, same result, different order. Let's look at the same exact moment i=0, k=1, j=0 so we can compare it directly to the naive version:
  • Still computing C[0][0]
  • Still grabbing A[0][1] = 2
  • Still grabbing B[1][0] = 3
But watch what happens as the innermost loop runs. Now j is the inner loop, so j increments (j=0 -> 1 -> 2)
For B[k][j]
  • B[1][0] → B[1][1] → B[1][2]
  • Flat memory positions: 1*N + 0, 1*N + 1, 1*N + 2
  • That's N, N+1, N+2 — consecutive positions in memory!
  • We're moving RIGHT across row 1 of B (that's the green highlighted row in the diagram)
One cache line = 64 bytes = 16 floats. Instead of wasting 15 floats every time, we now use all 16. That's where the theoretical 16x speedup comes from.
For C[i][j]:
  • Same thing C[0][0] -> C[0][1] -> C[0][2]
  • Also moving right, also sequential. (Purple highlight in the diagram)
Both B and C are now being accessed sequentially. Clean

Tiling

cpp
Matrix tiled_matmul(const Matrix& A, Matrix& B){
    if(A.columns != B.rows){
        std :: cout<< "The matrix multiplication is not possible due to dimensional mismatch";
        return Matrix();
    }

    const int tile = 32;
    int A_r = A.rows;
    int A_c = A.columns;
    int B_c = B.columns;
    Matrix result(A_r, B_c);
    result.zeros();

    for(int t_i = 0; t_i<A_r; t_i = t_i+tile){
        for(int t_j = 0; t_j<A_c; t_j = t_j+tile){
            for(int t_k = 0; t_k<B_c; t_k = t_k+tile){


                for(int i = t_i; i < t_i + tile; i++){
                    for(int k = t_k; k < t_k + tile; k++){
                        float A_val = A.at(i,k);
                        for(int j = t_j; j < t_j + tile; j++){
                            result.at(i,j) += A_val * B.at(k,j);
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return result;
}
Here is the cheat sheet on how to read the code -
  • The Outer Loops (t_i, t_j, t_k) are our block managers. They don't do any math they just move a 32x32 magnifying glass across our massive matrices. They select a specific chunk of Matrix A and a chunk of Matrix B, effectively saying, "Load these into the L1 cache."
  • The Inner Loops (i, k, j) are our familiar workhorses. Once the outer loops lock in a specific 32x32 block, these inner loops go to work. Notice that they are in the exact same i-k-j optimized order we built earlier
Wait, if i-k-j is so good, why do we need tiling?
That is the exact question I asked myself after I finished implementing the cache optimized version. So let me break it down. A 1024×1024 matrix of floats is exactly 4 Megabytes. But the L1 cache on most computers mine included is only 64KB. When we do matrix multiplication, we are dealing with three matrices (A, B, and the result C) which means we are juggling about 12MB of data. Even with perfect sequential access in the inner loop, the dataset simply doesn't fit. Here's what actually happens: as we iterate through the rows of A, each row of B gets loaded into the L1 cache. But by the time we move to the next row of A, that first row of B has already been evicted from the tiny 64KB cache to make room for other data. So we have to reload it. From RAM. Again.Let's look at the math -
For a 1024×1024 matrix, each row of B (4KB) gets loaded from RAM 1,024 times once for every single row of A. That is 4GB of slow RAM traffic just to multiply a 4MB matrix The i-k-j loop order made each individual access cache-friendly, but it didn't solve the reuse problem. Tiling fixes this. Instead of processing full matrices, we process small tiles that actually fit in L1. We load a 32×32 tile of A (4KB) and a 32×32 tile of B (4KB), and we do all the math on those two tiles before swapping either one out. Now, each tile of B gets loaded once and reused 32 times, instead of being evicted and reloaded 1,024 times that is a massive 32x reduction in RAM traffic.

Benchmarks

Done on a MacBook Air M3
So yeah, this is all CPU work. No CUDA yet. I haven't even touched a GPU kernel But that's the point I wanted to understand why loop order matters, why tiling works, and what the mental model feels like before I have to deal with explicit memory management on a GPU. Because here's the thing  the CUDA version is going to look almost identical to this. Same tiling strategy, same blocking, same idea of "load data into fast memory, do a bunch of work, swap it out."
